slides.title: Valid and invalid
slides.text:
Valid and invalid
Validity is a standard of correctness.
An invalid inference has made a mistake.
Valid
Invalid
If it is sunny, then ∀I is cycling
If it is sunny, then ∀I is cycling
It is sunny
∀I is cycling
∀I is cycling
It is sunny
The other premise is about the weather.
∀I also cycles in the rain.
They look alike. Logic wants a test that does not depend on a second look.
This mistake has a name: affirming the consequent.

slides.title: Truth preservation
slides.text:
Truth preservation
An inference is deductively valid iff the conclusion is true under
the (hypothetical) assumption that all the premises are true.
Hypothetical: we never check the premises.
So a valid inference can have false premises.
Imagine a world where cats fly. There the cat flies.
All cats can fly
Cats do not fly. The
∃I is a cat
reasoning is correct anyway.
∃I can fly
4
Validity relates truth-values. It does not report the facts.

slides.title: Valid, sound, true
slides.text:
Valid, sound, true
A sound argument is a deductively valid argument whose premises
are actually true. Its conclusion must therefore be true as well.
All cats can fly
All humans are mortal
If sunny, then ∀I cycles
∃I is a cat
Socrates is human
∀I is cycling
∃I can fly
Socrates is mortal
It is sunny
false premises
true premises
premises may be true
valid, not sound
valid and sound
not valid, not sound
Truth and validity come apart in every direction.
Logic checks the connection. Whether the premises hold is another question.

slides.title: Material validity
slides.text:
Material validity
Logically valid: truth preservation depends on the form.
Materially valid: it depends on what the words mean.
Carnap: add a meaning postulate
Sam is the brother of ∀I's mother
Sam is the brother of ∀I's mother
Sam is ∀I's uncle
The brother of a person's mother is their uncle
Sam is ∀I's uncle
Sam is the sister of ∀I's mother
Sam is ∀I's uncle
Now it follows by form alone.
then Sam is ∀I's aunt
Material too: n divisible by 4, so n even.
Logical validity is domain-general; material validity is domain-specific.

slides.title: Mostly: inductive validity
slides.text:
Mostly: inductive validity
"From a drop of water a logician
Inductively valid: the premises make the
could infer the possibility of an
conclusion likely, without guaranteeing it.
Atlantic or a Niagara."
A Study in Scarlet, 1887
How probable is C given the premises?
And how much do the premises raise it?
Holmes calls it deduction.
Almost all of it is induction.
Defeasible: smoke means fire, until you
hear that Mr. Sir smokes his pipe here.
Deduction accumulates beliefs; induction modulates them.
The evidence did not go away. It was supplemented, and that changed the conclusion.

slides.title: Enumerative induction
slides.text:
Enumerative induction
They're all white!!
All swans we have observed so far were white
All swans are white
All marbles we have drawn so far were white
the shared form
All marbles are white
All As we have observed so far were B
All As are B
The observations cannot lower the probability of C.
They do not make it likely either: size alone does not remove selection bias.

Careful: an inductive definition and an inductive inference are different things.

slides.title: Probabilities over models
slides.text:
Probabilities over models
In inductive logic, a model is a way the world could turn out.
One roll of a die: six models. A proposition is a set of them.
fair die
Pr(1) = … = Pr(6) = 1/6
Pr([EVEN]) = 1/2
[EVEN] = the models 2, 4 and 6
loaded die
A probability function gives each proposition a number
Pr(1) = … = Pr(5) = 1/10
between 0 and 1. The outcomes sum to 1.
Pr(6) = 1/2
Pr([EVEN]) = 7/10
Fixing the distribution is statistics; saying what it supports is logic.
